pages.text:
*Jun's phone says: home. Nari's river says: home.*

The sun was hot and dry, the kind that made the air shiver above the dirt road. The Long River lay quiet below the bank, its water a clear, bright green that reflected the blue sky without a single ripple. The red peppers in the yard stood in neat rows on the straw mats, glowing like rows of small, bright tomatoes that had forgotten they were spicy.

Jun stood by the door of the farmhouse. His suitcase leaned against the wall. It was no longer clean. A thick layer of brown mud had settled on the wheels and the sides, baking into the fabric and plastic. He looked at the stain. He reached out a hand, then pulled it back. If he brushed it off, the summer would be gone. If he left it, the summer was still in his pockets, in his sneakers, in the mud caked under his fingernails.

Halmoni was in the kitchen, the smell of sesame oil and rice drifting out to meet him. The house was quiet, except for the hum of a single cicada in the tree outside.
pages.image: Jun, a thin 12-year-old boy in round black-framed glasses and a white T-shirt, stands by a farmhouse door looking at his muddy suitcase, while bright red peppers dry on straw mats in the sunny yard behind him.

pages.text:
Halmoni emerged with a basket that seemed to contain the entire summer. She packed rice rolls in seaweed, then a whole watermelon, which did not fit and had to be balanced precariously on top. A jar of kimchi, wrapped in plastic and tied with string, went in next.

"Eat first. Talk later," she said, but she was already talking. "Chuseok is coming. In the autumn. The whole family will be here. You will come back."

Jun nodded. He felt a tightness in his chest, a feeling that was not quite sadness but was close to it.

Harabeoji stepped forward. He wore his faded green cap and his striped shirt. He did not say a lot of things, but when he did, they landed like stones in a still pond. He took Jun’s hand with both of his. His grip was dry and firm.

"Come back," he said.

Two words. It was a lot. It was enough.
pages.image: Halmoni, a small round woman in a floral top and purple sun visor, packs a large watermelon and a jar into a basket, while Harabeoji, a thin man in a green cap and striped shirt, holds Jun's hand with both of his.

pages.text:
The bus stop was under the rusty shelter, where the heat rose in waves. The cicadas screamed, a sound so loud it felt like it was inside Jun’s teeth. Nari stood there, her braid bouncing as she looked at him.

Jun reached into his pocket and pulled out a folded piece of paper. He had taped the torn score sheet back together. The ink was smudged, but under the old numbers, he had written a new heading.

"Look," he said, holding it out.

Nari took it. She unfolded it carefully. Under the line that had said *Nari 9, Jun 8*, there was a new line.

*US: 1*

Nari laughed. It was a real laugh, the kind that made her eyes crinkle. She reached into her pocket and pulled out a smooth, flat stone. On it, in black pen, was the faintest curve of a boat.

"For your window in Seoul," she said. "So the river can watch the city."
pages.image: Jun, a thin boy in round glasses, holds out a folded paper to Nari, a sunburnt girl with a long black braid and a straw hat, who is smiling at him under a rusty bus shelter in bright sunlight.

pages.text:
The bus horn honked in the distance, a sharp blast that cut through the endless hum of the cicadas.

Jun took a step forward, his muddy sneakers leaving a dark print on the dusty road. "I'll take you to Seoul," he said, pushing his glasses up his nose. "Winter break. You'll see the subway."

Nari tilted her head, her braid sliding over her shoulder. "I'll check it out first."

"You'll hate the buildings," Jun said, trying to sound casual. "They're too tall. Too loud."

"I'll love the buildings," Nari said, and she grinned. It was a challenge, but it was also a promise. "Then I'll tell you why they're wrong."

Jun grinned back, feeling the heat in his chest. He picked up his suitcase, the mud still heavy on the wheels. He looked at the girl who had once thought he was helpless, and the boy who had once thought she was stuck in the past. They were not those people anymore. They were the people who had pulled the boat through the dark.

"See you in the autumn," he said.

"See you," she said.
pages.image: Jun, a thin boy in round glasses and a white T-shirt, grins at Nari, a sunburnt girl with a long black braid and a yellow T-shirt, as they stand by a moving bus in a dusty village road.

pages.text:
The bus pulled away, kicking up a cloud of brown dust that hung in the air for a long time. Jun’s face was at the window, watching until the trees and the valley and the girl with the long braid were all hidden by the swirl of dirt and light.

Nari stood still for a moment. Then she turned and walked home along the riverbank. The water was clear and moving, carrying leaves and small twigs downstream. She put her hands in her pockets. In one, the smooth stone sat against her palm. In the other, a small piece of paper with Jun’s phone number, written in his neat, careful handwriting.

She stopped. She sniffed the air and squinted at the sky.

"Clear till Thursday," she said to nobody.

She looked at the paper. She smiled. Then she walked on, her shadow long and thin on the hot ground.
pages.image: Nari, a sunburnt girl with a long black braid and a straw hat on her back, walks alone along a clear green riverbank in bright sunlight, holding a small piece of paper in her hand.
